section.title: Priests and Prophets
section.sectionRationale: This chapter contrasts Israel's God-given offices, the priest and the prophet, with the detestable divination of the nations, and climaxes in the LORD's promise to raise up a prophet like Moses, a hinge text the apostles later applied directly to Jesus.
section.thesis: Because Israel must not seek hidden knowledge through pagan divination, the LORD provides two true channels of access to Himself: the Levitical priesthood, whose only inheritance is the LORD, and, above all, a prophet like Moses whom the New Testament identifies as Jesus Christ, tested by whether his word comes true.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the priests' portion; the ban on divination and the detestable practices of the nations; the promise of a prophet like Moses; and the test for recognizing a true prophet's word.

units.label: The priests' portion
units.note: the LORD Himself is their inheritance

verses.text: The Levitical priests, indeed the whole tribe of Levi, shall have no portion or inheritance with Israel. They are to eat the offerings made by fire to the LORD; that is their inheritance.
Although they have no inheritance among their brothers, the LORD is their inheritance, as He promised them.
This shall be the priests' share from the people who offer a sacrifice, whether a bull or a sheep: the priests are to be given the shoulder, the jowls, and the stomach.
You are to give them the firstfruits of your grain, new wine, and oil, and the first wool sheared from your flock.
For the LORD your God has chosen Levi and his sons out of all your tribes to stand and minister in His name for all time.
Now if a Levite moves from any town of residence throughout Israel and comes in all earnestness to the place the LORD will choose,
then he shall serve in the name of the LORD his God like all his fellow Levites who stand there before the LORD.
They shall eat equal portions, even though he has received money from the sale of his father's estate.

units.label: No divination, only the LORD
units.note: the detestable practices of the nations

verses.text: When you enter the land that the LORD your God is giving you, do not imitate the detestable ways of the nations there.
Let no one be found among you who sacrifices his son or daughter in the fire, practices divination or conjury, interprets omens, practices sorcery,
casts spells, consults a medium or spiritist, or inquires of the dead.
For whoever does these things is {{toebah|detestable}} to the LORD. And because of these detestable things, the LORD your God is driving out the nations before you.
You must be {{tamim|blameless}} before the LORD your God.
Though these nations, which you will dispossess, listen to conjurers and diviners, the LORD your God has not permitted you to do so.

units.label: A prophet like Moses
units.note: the LORD's provision for the fear at Horeb

verses.text: The LORD your God will raise up for you a {{navi|prophet}} like me from among your brothers. You must listen to him.

This is what you asked of the LORD your God at Horeb on the day of the assembly, when you said, "Let us not hear the voice of the LORD our God or see this great fire anymore, so that we will not die!"
Then the LORD said to me, "They have spoken well.
I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. I will put My words in his mouth, and he will tell them everything I command him.
And I will hold accountable anyone who does not listen to My words that the prophet speaks in My name.
But if any prophet dares to speak a message in My name that I have not commanded him to speak, or to speak in the name of other gods, that prophet must be put to death."
You may ask in your heart, "How can we recognize a message that the LORD has not spoken?"

When a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD and the message does not come to pass or come true, that is a message the LORD has not spoken. The prophet has spoken presumptuously. Do not be afraid of him.

navi.gloss: A prophet, one who speaks on behalf of another. A navi does not originate a message but delivers exactly what God has put in his mouth. The office finds its perfect and final fulfillment in Christ, the ultimate Prophet, Acts 3:22-23.

toebah.gloss: Detestable, an abomination, something that violates the LORD's character and order. Applied here to child sacrifice and every form of divination, the very practices the surrounding nations built their religion on.

tamim.gloss: Blameless, complete, whole-hearted. Israel is called to undivided loyalty to the LORD rather than hedging their trust with pagan divination on the side.

basic.context: Moses turns from land and leadership laws to two offices that mediate God's presence to Israel: the priesthood, who serve at the altar with no inheritance but the LORD Himself, and prophecy, God's answer to the divination and sorcery that surrounded Israel in Canaan. The chapter closes with a stunning promise: God will raise up a prophet like Moses.
basic.hermeneutics: This is genuinely about ancient Israel's priests and its coming prophetic office, but Peter and Stephen both treat the prophet like Moses as a direct prophecy of Jesus, not merely a loose pattern (Acts 3:22-23, 7:37). The ban on occult practices also speaks honestly into today's forms of the same temptation, seeking hidden knowledge or power apart from God's revealed word.
basic.originalLanguages: The navi, prophet, does not invent a message but speaks only what God puts in his mouth. Israel is called to be tamim, blameless or whole-hearted, rather than divided between the LORD and pagan divination. The forbidden practices are toebah, a strong word for whatever violates God's order and character.
basic.typology: Moses himself, the mediator who spoke with God directly, becomes the pattern for every true prophet after him, and supremely for Christ, who speaks the very words of God perfectly and finally, Hebrews 1:1-2.
basic.christ: Verse 15's promised prophet is explicitly applied to Jesus in Acts 3:22-23 and 7:37: he is the greater Moses, whose words carry the full authority of God and whose rejection brings judgment, verse 19.
basic.god: God does not leave His people to grope after hidden knowledge through divination; He speaks plainly. He provides for their real needs, priests to mediate access and a prophet to speak His words directly, so they need not fear or manipulate unseen powers.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 3:22-23 and 7:37 apply the prophet like Moses directly to Jesus. Hebrews 1:1-2 says God has spoken finally by His Son. 1 Corinthians 10:20 warns that pagan sacrifices are offered to demons, not empty nothings.
basic.oneStory: From the priesthood's atoning access and the prophet's authoritative word, the whole Bible moves toward the one who is final Prophet, Priest, and King, Jesus Christ, in whom God's speech to His people reaches its fullness.

context.literary:
The chapter's four movements are arranged around a single question: how does Israel legitimately learn what God wants. Priesthood answers that question through sacrifice and portion (18:1-8); prophecy answers it through spoken word (18:15-22); and sandwiched between the two stands the list of illegitimate shortcuts, every form of divination the nations practiced (18:9-14). The structure itself makes the point before a single word of application is offered, true access to God comes only through what He appoints, never through what a person contrives.

The word toebah, detestable, forms a small hinge back to the previous chapter. It names the blemished sacrifice and the sacred pillar in 17:1 and 16:22, and it names the whole list of occult practices again in 18:9,12, binding chapters 17 and 18 into one continuous warning against every counterfeit way of approaching God, whether through a corrupted altar or a consulted spirit.

The most striking literary move comes in verses 16 to 18, where Moses stops narrating and starts quoting. Up to that point he has spoken to Israel in the second person, 'you' will do this, 'you' must not do that. Then, without warning, he reports God's own first person words back to him at Horeb, 'I will raise up for them a prophet... I will put My words in his mouth.' The text embodies its own claim: a true prophet is someone who can, and does, hand on the exact words spoken to him rather than paraphrase or improve on them, and Moses demonstrates the pattern in the very act of quoting God rather than summarizing Him.

The chapter then closes by returning to instruction, giving Israel a public, checkable test rather than asking for blind trust in whoever claims the prophetic office. Structure and content agree throughout, legitimate revelation is always traceable, testable, and given, never hidden, manipulated, or assumed.
context.historical:
Priests in the ancient Near East commonly held vast temple estates, land grants from kings, and independent economic power that made them a political force in their own right. Levi received none of this. The tribe's only land was forty eight scattered towns (Numbers 35:1-8), and its livelihood depended entirely on the portions and tithes described in verses 3-4, a structural choice that kept the priesthood dependent on Israel's faithfulness rather than on independent wealth.

The list of forbidden practices in verses 10-11 names real, well attested technologies of the ancient world. Mesopotamian courts kept professional diviners who read the shape of a sacrificed animal's liver, tracked astrological omens, and consulted written omen collections before major decisions. Necromancy, inquiring of the dead, appears vividly in Israel's own later history when Saul, desperate and abandoned by God's silence, seeks out a medium at Endor to raise Samuel (1 Samuel 28:3-19), a scene that reads like a direct violation of this very law by Israel's own first king. Child sacrifice 'in the fire' is likewise attested archaeologically in the wider Levant and is condemned repeatedly elsewhere in the Torah and the prophets as a defining horror of Canaanite religion.

Against this background, Israel's alternative looks almost austere. No royal astrologers, no state necromancers, no professional guild claiming secret access to hidden knowledge. Only a priesthood living off the people's offerings and a prophet who says nothing except what he has been told to say, tested publicly by whether his words come true. The comparative poverty of Israel's system, no temple estates, no arcane technique, was itself a statement about the character of the God who required it.
context.canonical:
Numbers 18:20 supplies the fuller version of the LORD-as-portion language this chapter compresses, telling Aaron directly, 'You shall have no inheritance in their land, nor will you have any portion among them; I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites.' Centuries later, worshippers personalize that priestly language for themselves, 'the LORD is my chosen portion' (Psalm 16:5) and 'the LORD is my portion, therefore I will wait for Him' (Lamentations 3:24), showing that what began as Levi's unique arrangement became every believer's confession.

The ban on consulting the dead becomes a live issue almost immediately. Saul's visit to the medium at Endor (1 Samuel 28) is presented as the final proof of his rejection, and Isaiah later mocks the same impulse directly, 'should not a people inquire of their God? Why consult the dead on behalf of the living?' (Isaiah 8:19). The test for a true prophet in verses 21-22 also becomes a live wire running through the prophetic books: Jeremiah's confrontation with Hananiah ends with Hananiah's death exactly as Jeremiah had predicted (Jeremiah 28:15-17), and Deuteronomy 13's separate test, whether a prophet's teaching leads Israel toward or away from the LORD, works alongside this chapter's test of fulfillment rather than against it.

The New Testament treats verse 15 as the hinge on which the whole Old Testament prophetic office turns. Peter and Stephen both quote it directly of Jesus, but even before either speech, the voice at the Transfiguration applies its very language, 'listen to him,' to Jesus in the hearing of Peter, James, and John (Matthew 17:5), making this chapter's promise something the apostles heard fulfilled with their own ears before they ever preached it.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses is closing off every backdoor into Canaan's religion before Israel ever crosses the Jordan. The nations Israel is about to dispossess ran their whole religious life on hidden knowledge, extracted from a liver, a star chart, or a consulted ghost, and Moses knows the same hunger for control over an uncertain future will tempt Israel the moment ordinary life gets hard. His aim is not simply to forbid a list of practices but to starve the appetite behind them, the wish to know and manage the future apart from trusting the God who already knows it.

He replaces that appetite with something Israel can actually rely on: priests who mediate access at the altar and, when needed, a true prophet who speaks God's own words rather than a diviner's guesswork. By telling Israel exactly how to test a prophet's claim, whether the word comes to pass, Moses also intends to protect the office he is establishing from the very abuse he has just condemned, so that a true prophet can never be mistaken for one more voice competing with the diviners he was raised up to replace.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The specific priestly income, the shoulder, jowls, and stomach of every sacrifice, firstfruits of grain, wine, oil, and wool, describes Israel's old covenant support system for the Levites and is not a template for funding ministry today, though the underlying principle, that those who serve at the altar should be materially supported by those they serve, carries forward explicitly into Paul's own argument for supporting gospel workers (1 Corinthians 9:13-14).

The death penalty for presumptuous false prophecy likewise belonged to Israel's unique civil and covenant order and is not a pattern for how the church treats false teaching now. What is prescriptive and abiding is the test itself: any claim to speak for God must be checked against what actually happens and against Scripture's own content, never simply accepted on the strength of the speaker's confidence or charisma. John's warning to 'test the spirits to see whether they are from God' (1 John 4:1) applies this chapter's logic to every era, even where the specific penalty no longer does.

debates.question: Is Deuteronomy 18:15-19 about a single individual or an ongoing prophetic succession?

views.label: Primarily an ongoing succession
views.case: The near context concerns a continuing line of true prophets replacing pagan divination, since Israel would need prophetic guidance for centuries, and Deuteronomy 34:10 notes that 'no prophet has risen in Israel like Moses' up to that point, implying the office continued to be filled by many.

views.label: A climactic, singular fulfillment
views.case: Peter (Acts 3:22-23) and Stephen (Acts 7:37) apply the text pointedly to Jesus alone as the definitive, greater Moses, and the voice at the Transfiguration echoes the chapter's own command, 'listen to him' (Matthew 17:5), suggesting the whole line of prophets was itself pointing toward one final Prophet.

debates.bearing: Both are true together: God raised up many true prophets, and that whole succession finds its terminus and fulfillment in Jesus, the Prophet like Moses in the fullest sense.

debates.question: Does fulfillment alone, the test given in verses 21-22, settle whether a prophet is true, given that Deuteronomy 13:1-3 warns that even a prophet whose sign comes true must be rejected if he leads Israel toward other gods?

views.label: Two complementary tests, not one
views.case: Chapter 18 addresses the prophet who presumes to speak without any word from God at all, a false claim to inspiration exposed by failed fulfillment. Chapter 13 addresses a different danger, someone whose prediction does come true yet still calls Israel to worship other gods. Read together, Israel is taught to test both whether a word comes to pass and whether it leads toward or away from the LORD, since either test alone could be deceived.

views.label: Fulfillment as the primary but not sole criterion
views.case: Some read chapter 18's test as the chapter's main concern, distinguishing genuine prophecy from empty presumption, while treating chapter 13 as an extreme, deliberately engineered exception meant to show that no single test, not even a fulfilled sign, can override loyalty to the God already revealed.

debates.bearing: Either way, Israel is never meant to rely on a single mechanical check. A true word from God will both come to pass and call God's people more deeply toward Him, never away, and the two chapters guard against opposite errors, gullibility toward failed prediction and gullibility toward accurate but idolatrous prediction.

study.originalLanguages:
Verses 1 and 2 pair two different Hebrew words for what a person owns. Chelek is a portion or share, the cut of meat or produce a priest actually receives (verse 8 uses the same root, 'equal portions'). Nachalah is something deeper, an inheritance, the allotted, permanent possession tied to land and to family identity that every other tribe received when Canaan was divided. Levi is denied nachalah in the ordinary sense, yet the text does not leave the word behind, it simply relocates it, 'the LORD is their nachalah.' The tribe with no land inheritance is given the deepest possible inheritance instead.

Verse 10's list of forbidden practices includes one who 'inquires of the dead,' doresh el hammethim, built on the verb darash, to seek, inquire, or search out. Deuteronomy uses this identical verb elsewhere in a wholly positive sense, promising that Israel 'will seek the LORD your God' and find Him if they search with all their heart (4:29). The chapter is not condemning the impulse to seek answers; it is condemning where that search is aimed, at the dead instead of at the living God.

In verse 18, God's promise that He will 'put My words in his mouth' uses the verb natan, to give or put, in a construction identical to His later commissioning of Jeremiah, 'I have put My words in your mouth' (Jeremiah 1:9). The repetition of this exact verbal phrase across centuries suggests a fixed, recognizable formula for genuine prophetic call, distinguishing an appointed spokesman from anyone simply claiming inspiration.

Verse 20's 'dares to speak,' yazid, comes from the root zud, to boil over or act presumptuously, the same root behind Esau's boiling stew in Genesis 25:29 and behind the earlier warning in 17:12 against the man who 'acts presumptuously' toward the priest or judge. Deuteronomy reuses this single root to describe both contempt for a lawful court and false claims to speak for God, treating them as the same underlying sin, an inflated self-confidence that refuses to submit to what has actually been given.

Finally, the mediums and spiritists of verse 11 are named with two distinct Hebrew terms, ov, most likely the ritual pit or vessel through which a spirit was consulted, and yidde'oni, literally 'one who knows,' a title claiming secret knowledge the practitioner did not actually possess. The very names of these forbidden offices advertise the counterfeit at the center of the whole list, a false claim to know what only God truly knows.

typology.type: The Levite whose only portion is the LORD Himself (18:1-2)
typology.fulfillment: Levi's landlessness becomes, in time, a description any believer can claim. The psalmist takes up the very phrase for himself, 'the LORD is my chosen portion' (Psalm 16:5), and Lamentations 3:24 personalizes it further still amid national ruin. The pattern reaches its height in Christ our great high priest, who 'holds His priesthood permanently' and always lives to intercede, needing no earthly inheritance because His own portion, and ours in Him, is God Himself forever (Hebrews 7:23-25). The type falls short in one respect, Levi's landlessness was involuntary and structural, while Christ's identical portion is willingly and eternally His own.

typology.type: The ban on inquiring of the dead on behalf of the living (18:10-11)
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah later sharpens this ban into a question, 'should not a people inquire of their God? Why consult the dead on behalf of the living?' (Isaiah 8:19). Jesus answers that question by becoming the one living voice no grave can silence, declaring 'I am the resurrection and the life' (John 11:25). Where the nations sought the dead to learn about the living, the gospel announces a Living One who was dead and now lives forever. The correspondence is not a direct fulfillment so much as a resolution, the entire practice this law forbids is rendered unnecessary once the true source of life and knowledge has conquered death itself.

typology.type: God putting His own words into the prophet's mouth (18:18)
typology.fulfillment: The formula recurs almost verbatim at Jeremiah's call, 'I have put My words in your mouth' (Jeremiah 1:9), marking every true prophet as a mouthpiece rather than an originator. Jesus describes His own ministry in the same terms taken to their limit, 'My teaching is not My own... I do not speak on My own accord, but the Father who sent Me has commanded Me what to say' (John 12:49, 7:16). Every prophet before Him could only relay borrowed words imperfectly; the Son speaks the Father's words because He and the Father are one, closing the gap the type could only point toward.

typology.type: The test of whether a prophet's word comes to pass (18:21-22)
typology.fulfillment: Every claim to speak for God in this chapter stands or falls on a single, checkable outcome. Jesus repeatedly submits Himself to the same test in advance, predicting His own death and resurrection in specific, falsifiable terms (Matthew 16:21), then fulfilling them exactly, as even His opponents remembered, 'after three days I will rise again' (Matthew 27:63, John 2:19-22). No pretender in Scripture survives this test at that scale. The type escalates rather than merely repeats, since ordinary prophets were tested on isolated predictions, while Christ was tested on His own death and resurrection, the two events on which the entire gospel depends.

study.christ:
The most striking thread from this chapter to Christ is not simply the direct quotation in Acts, but an echo most readers miss on a first reading. Verse 16 recalls Israel's terror at Horeb, begging Moses that they might 'not hear the voice of the LORD our God or see this great fire anymore.' Centuries later, on another mountain, Peter, James, and John hear a voice from a cloud say of Jesus exactly what this chapter commands Israel to do toward the promised prophet, 'This is My beloved Son... Listen to Him' (Matthew 17:5, echoed at Luke 9:35). The apostles are not merely told that Jesus fulfills an ancient promise. They are personally handed the very command this chapter gives, and told to obey it toward Him.

The chapter's logic of derived speech also finds its limit in Christ. A true prophet never originates a message; he only carries one. Jesus describes His own ministry the same way, taken to a degree no ordinary prophet could claim, 'the words I say to you I do not speak on My own accord... My teaching is not My own; it is from the One who sent Me' (John 14:10, 7:16). John's opening chapter frames the whole relationship between this book and its fulfillment in a single sentence, 'the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ' (John 1:17). Moses reported words given to him; Christ, as the eternal Word, is Himself the message.

The chapter's warning also has an edge that lands on Christ's hearers directly. Verse 19 promises that God will personally hold accountable anyone who refuses to listen to His true prophet's words. That is precisely the danger Jesus presses on His own contemporaries, warning that rejecting Him is not a neutral act of disbelief but a refusal of the very voice this chapter told Israel to obey above every other, including their own fear of hearing God directly.

Finally, the test of a true prophet, whether his word comes to pass, finds its ultimate proving ground at the cross and the empty tomb. Jesus predicted His own death and resurrection with specific enough detail that even His enemies remembered the claim and tried to guard against it (Matthew 27:62-66), and its exact fulfillment three days later stands as the largest scale demonstration in Scripture of the very test this chapter sets for every prophet who came before Him.
study.god:
This chapter reveals a God who refuses to leave His people groping in the dark, yet also refuses to be managed. He does not withhold guidance the way the pagan mind imagined its gods did, forcing desperate people to bribe or manipulate hidden powers through divination. He speaks plainly, through appointed priests and, when needed, a true prophet, and He does so precisely so that His people never have to consult a grave, a liver, or a star chart to find out what He wants.

At the same time, He is jealous for the integrity of His own name. Verse 19 warns that He will personally hold accountable anyone who ignores His true spokesman's words, and verse 20 sets a capital penalty on anyone who dares to invent a message and attribute it to Him. A God who speaks so generously will not tolerate His own words being counterfeited, because a fabricated word spoken in His name does not merely mislead people, it slanders Him.

His provision for the priesthood tells the same story from another angle. The Levites hold no land, yet God calls Himself their portion and their inheritance, meaning His own generosity, not a plot of ground, guarantees their future. He is a God who supplies real, ongoing material need, the shoulder, the firstfruits, the wool, while insisting that ultimate security rests in Him rather than in any possession, a lesson every tribe with land was also meant to learn by watching the one tribe without it.

For worship, this chapter teaches that trusting God means refusing every shortcut to certainty that bypasses His actual revealed word, however comforting or urgent the temptation to seek one out might feel. It also teaches confidence, since the God who forbids consulting the dead for hidden knowledge is the same God who has already promised to keep speaking through a true prophet, so that His people are never actually left without a trustworthy word when they need one.

crossReferences.note: Gives the fuller version of the priestly portion language this chapter compresses, God telling Aaron directly and personally that He Himself is Levi's portion and inheritance rather than any share of land.

David personalizes the very language given to the landless Levites, calling the LORD his own chosen portion and inheritance, showing how this priestly promise became every ordinary believer's confession too.
Isaiah mocks the impulse this chapter forbids directly, asking why a people would consult the dead on behalf of the living instead of simply inquiring of their own faithful and living God.
Saul's visit to the medium at Endor to consult the dead Samuel is presented by the narrator as the clearest violation of this chapter's ban and the final, decisive proof of Saul's rejection as king.
God tells Jeremiah, 'I have put My words in your mouth,' echoing this chapter's promise about the true prophet almost word for word and marking Jeremiah out plainly as its kind of spokesman.
The false prophet Hananiah dies within the very year Jeremiah predicted his death, a vivid example of this chapter's test for a true prophet's word actually playing out in real historical time.
Sets a second test alongside this chapter's test of fulfillment, warning that even a prophet whose sign comes true must still be rejected outright if his message leads Israel toward other gods.

At the Transfiguration a voice from heaven commands Peter, James, and John to 'listen to Him' concerning Jesus, applying this chapter's very own command about the promised prophet directly in the apostles' hearing.

Jesus describes His own teaching as entirely given Him by the Father rather than self originated, embodying to the fullest possible degree the pattern of a prophet who speaks only what he has been told.

Malachi rebukes a later generation of priests for despising the very offerings this chapter assigns them, showing plainly how far the priesthood had drifted from its own founding, God given provision.

study.oneStory:
The very first lie in Scripture was a kind of divination in disguise. The serpent offered Eve hidden knowledge, 'your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil' (Genesis 3:5), a promise of secret insight gained apart from trusting what God had actually said. Every practice this chapter forbids, reading a liver, consulting a corpse, casting a spell, is a descendant of that same original offer, the appeal of knowing what only God knows without having to trust Him for it.

Against that ancient temptation, God builds two lawful channels into Israel's life, a priesthood that mediates access to Him through appointed sacrifice, and a prophetic word that tells His people what He actually wants without any secret technique required. Both offices are, by design, limited and dependent, the priest lives off the people's offerings rather than his own estate, and the prophet speaks only what has been given him rather than what he invents. Neither office lets a human being become the source of divine knowledge.

Israel's later history shows how easily both offices could still be corrupted, priests despising their own table (Malachi 1:6-14) and kings consulting mediums in open defiance of this very law (1 Samuel 28). Yet the prophetic line never goes silent, running from Samuel through Elijah, Isaiah, and Jeremiah, each one tested by whether his word came true, until it reaches the one Prophet whose every word was vindicated beyond dispute by His own death and resurrection.

The story does not end with a better priest and a better prophet merely replacing the old ones. It ends with access to God made so complete that the entire structure this chapter protects, a mediated portion, a tested word, gives way to unmediated presence. John's closing vision pictures a people who will 'see His face' and need no more lamp or sun, 'for the Lord God will shine on them' (Revelation 22:4-5), the hidden knowledge Eden's serpent once promised finally, rightly, and freely given by the God who was never keeping it back.

sermon.title: Jesus Vs. the Occult
sermon.why: Piper works directly through Deuteronomy 18:9-14 on the ban on occult practices and then to verses 15-19, explicitly naming Jesus as the fulfillment of the prophet like Moses through Acts 3:22-23, making it a strong match for this chapter's full argument.

quiz.q: What is given as the priests' true inheritance in this chapter?

options.text: The LORD Himself, rather than a portion of land like the other tribes.
options.note: Verses 1-2 explicitly state that the LORD is Levi's inheritance.

options.text: A double portion of every sacrifice offered by the people.
options.note: The priests do receive a real share of the offerings, verses 3-4, but that is not what the text calls their 'inheritance'; that term is reserved for the LORD Himself.

options.text: Land taken from the Canaanite nations.
options.note: The Levites specifically receive no land inheritance among their brothers, verse 1.

options.text: Nothing at all; they were left to fend for themselves.
options.note: Verses 3-5 describe real, commanded provision from the offerings and firstfruits.

quiz.q: According to this chapter, what practices does the LORD forbid Israel from imitating?

options.text: Child sacrifice, divination, sorcery, and consulting mediums or the dead.
options.note: Verses 10-11 list these detestable practices in detail.

options.text: Only child sacrifice.
options.note: Child sacrifice heads the list, but verses 10-11 name several other occult practices as well.

options.text: Eating certain foods.
options.note: That is not the subject of this passage; see chapter 14 for dietary laws.

options.text: Nothing; the chapter gives no such prohibition.
options.note: Verses 9-12 give an explicit, detailed prohibition.

quiz.q: Why would God raise up a prophet like Moses, according to verse 16?

options.text: Because the people themselves asked at Horeb not to hear God's voice directly, fearing they would die.
options.note: Verse 16 recalls the people's own request at Horeb for a mediator.

options.text: Because Moses requested it for himself before he died.
options.note: The origin is the people's fear at Horeb, not a personal request from Moses.

options.text: Because the priests were unable to teach the law.
options.note: The priesthood's function is addressed earlier; the prophet answers the people's fear of hearing God directly.

options.text: For no stated reason.
options.note: Verse 16 gives an explicit reason rooted in Israel's own request at Horeb.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament identify the prophet like Moses?

options.text: As Jesus Christ, quoted directly by Peter in Acts 3:22-23.
options.note: Peter applies this prophecy explicitly to the risen Christ.

options.text: As John the Baptist.
options.note: John pointed to Christ, but the New Testament reserves this specific title for Jesus Himself.

options.text: As an unfulfilled promise still awaited.
options.note: Acts 3 treats the prophecy as already fulfilled in Jesus.

options.text: The New Testament never addresses this prophecy.
options.note: Acts 3:22-23 and 7:37 both directly cite it.

quiz.q: What is the test for whether a prophet has truly spoken from the LORD?

options.text: Whether the message comes to pass or comes true.
options.note: Verse 22 gives this explicit test.

options.text: Whether the prophet is popular with the people.
options.note: Popularity is never given as the test; fulfillment is.

options.text: Whether the prophet performs miracles.
options.note: Miracles are not the test given here; the fulfillment of the specific word is.

options.text: There is no test given.
options.note: Verse 22 gives an explicit and clear test.

questions: Israel was tempted to seek hidden knowledge through divination rather than trust God's revealed word. Where are you tempted to look for guidance outside of what God has actually said?
The Levites' portion was the LORD Himself, not land. What would change in your life if you treasured God Himself above the things He gives?
God promised a prophet whose words carried His full authority, fulfilled in Jesus. How seriously do you take the words of Christ compared with other voices competing for your trust?
The people at Horeb were too afraid to hear God's voice directly and asked for a mediator. How does having Christ as your mediator change your posture toward God, fear or confidence?
A true prophet's words always came to pass. Where do you need to test the promises you are relying on against what God has actually said in Scripture?

translationNotes.note: The list of forbidden practices, divination, conjury, omens, sorcery, spells, mediums, spiritists, necromancy, uses several overlapping Hebrew terms for occult activity; translators vary in exact English equivalents, but the cumulative sense is a total ban on seeking hidden knowledge from anyone but the LORD.

'A prophet like me' can be read collectively, an ongoing line of prophets, or singularly, one final prophet; the New Testament reads it climactically of Christ without denying the intervening line of true prophets.
'I will hold accountable' translates a Hebrew idiom of personal reckoning, underscoring that rejecting God's true spokesman is treated as rejecting God Himself.
